Scenes 4 and 5: use short example clips with real artifacts generated by the team in Google Flow or Kling during Stage 4 (for example a hand with extra fingers, a flickering texture, a sign with random letters). Do not use clips taken from other creators.
Scene 12 slide can show still frames from Priya's six shots if the team generates them; otherwise use simple icons for each shot. The electricity meter graphic must show generic numbers, no brand.
Priya and the solar installer in Pune are hypothetical; stock footage must show no real company name or logo.

Hook.voiceover: You now have a folder full of clips. Some are excellent, some are strange, and some are almost right. The skill today is not generating more clips. It is deciding, quickly and with reasons, what to do with the clips you have.

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, you added an avatar presenter. Now it is time to review everything you have made so far.

slide.title: Diagnosing Artifacts: Regenerate, Edit or Replace?
slide.body: AI Video Production and Motion · Lesson 10 of 14

Explain.voiceover: An artifact is a visual error caused by the generation process. There are five common types. Warped hands and faces. Melting or morphing objects. Flicker. Unreadable text. And physics that looks wrong.

slide.title: Five common artifacts
slide.body: Warped hands and faces · Melting or morphing objects · Flicker · Unreadable text · Wrong physics

Explain.voiceover: Let's look closer. Hands may have extra fingers, or fingers that merge. A cup changes shape, or a bicycle wheel bends. Flicker is when light, colours or textures jump from frame to frame.

slide.title: What they look like, part 1
slide.body: Three still frames with a red circle on each problem: a hand with an extra finger · a cup changing shape across two frames · a textured wall with a patch that jumps in brightness.

Explain.voiceover: Unreadable text means signs and labels with letters that do not form words. And wrong physics means water flowing upwards, people walking without moving forward, or objects passing through each other.

slide.title: What they look like, part 2
slide.body: Two still frames with red circles: a shop sign with random letter shapes · a person's arm passing through a railing.

Explain.voiceover: How do you review? Watch each clip at full size, at least twice. Then step through the problem areas slowly, or pause at several points. Many artifacts appear only for a moment, but viewers notice them on a large screen.
Explain.stock_query: person reviewing video frame by frame on monitor

Explain.voiceover: Now the decision guide. For each clip, choose one of four actions. Keep it, when there are no visible problems at normal speed. Trim it, when the problem is only at the start or end, and the good part is long enough.

slide.title: Decision guide, part 1
slide.body: Keep: no visible problems at normal speed · Trim: problem only at the start or end, and the good part is long enough

Explain.voiceover: Regenerate it, when the problem runs through the clip and a prompt change could fix it, like less motion or a simpler action. And replace it when several attempts have failed, or the shot needs readable text. Use a graphic, a still with a slow zoom, a licensed stock clip, or your own footage.

slide.title: Decision guide, part 2
slide.body: Regenerate: problem runs through the clip; try less motion, a simpler action or a keyframe · Replace: attempts failed or readable text needed; use a graphic, a still with slow zoom, licensed stock or your own footage

Explain.voiceover: You can also crop. Reframing a clip in the editor can remove a problem at the edge of the picture, if the quality stays good enough. And set a limit, such as three regenerations per shot. After that, replacing is usually faster and cheaper.

slide.title: Crop, and set a limit
slide.body: Left: a frame with a problem at the edge and a crop box around the main subject. Right: a counter showing 1, 2, 3 regenerations, then an arrow to 'replace'.

Explain.voiceover: Think of a doctor at a clinic. Some patients need nothing. Some need a small treatment, some need a second test, and some need a specialist. The doctor does not keep repeating a test that already failed three times.
Explain.stock_query: doctor talking with patient in clinic

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see an example. Priya is producing a seventy-second explainer about rooftop solar panels for a small installer in Pune, India. The installer is made up for this lesson. She reviews six clips.
Demonstrate.stock_query: solar panels on city rooftop sunrise

Demonstrate.voiceover: Shot one, a wide city at sunrise, is clean, so she keeps it. In shot two, a technician's hand has six fingers for about one second in the middle. She will regenerate, with the hands out of frame and the focus on the panel.

slide.title: Shots 1 and 2
slide.body: Shot 1: wide city at sunrise → Keep (clean). Shot 2: hand with six fingers mid-clip → Regenerate ('hands out of frame', focus on the panel).

Demonstrate.voiceover: In shot three, the panels flicker in the last two seconds. The first four seconds are clean, so she trims it. In shot four, an electricity meter shows random symbols. Readable numbers need a graphic, so she replaces it with a simple animation made in the editor.

slide.title: Shots 3 and 4
slide.body: Shot 3: flicker in the last 2 s → Trim (first 4 s are clean). Shot 4: meter shows random symbols → Replace with a simple animated graphic.

Demonstrate.voiceover: In shot five, a child's arm passes through a railing. After three failed attempts, she uses a still keyframe with a slow zoom. In shot six, a bird near the edge melts. A slight crop removes it.

slide.title: Shots 5 and 6
slide.body: Shot 5: arm passes through a railing → Regenerate × 3, then Replace with a still and slow zoom. Shot 6: bird melts at the edge → Crop.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Now Priya knows exactly which shots need more work, and which ones are ready for the edit.

slide.title: Priya's review
slide.body: Table of 6 rows with coloured tags: 1 Keep · 2 Regenerate · 3 Trim · 4 Replace · 5 Replace · 6 Crop. Two columns below: ready for the edit (1, 3, 4, 5, 6) · needs work (2).

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to keep every clip because you spent credits on it. Another is to regenerate every problem again and again, hoping for perfection. Both waste time. A simple still or graphic is often the best choice.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: A still is often the best choice

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, common artifacts are warped hands and faces, melting objects, flicker, unreadable text and wrong physics. Second, for each clip, decide to keep, trim, regenerate or replace, and write a reason. Third, set a regeneration limit, and replace shots that need readable text or keep failing.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Five artifacts: hands and faces · melting · flicker · text · physics. 2. Keep, trim, regenerate or replace, with a reason. 3. Set a limit; replace text shots and repeat failures.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. Put all your clips in one folder, and review each one at full size. Mark it keep, trim, regenerate or replace, with a reason. Keep your table, because you will need it for your capstone production note. It takes about twenty-five minutes. Next lesson: Editing in CapCut, Assembly, Pacing and Captions.
